Ideally, the system gives its reasons the way a botanist would: toothed edge, simple leaf, alternate → American beech.

How it works: two YOLO levels between photo and field guide

1Photo
iNaturalist
photos uploaded in 2026
→
2Leaf-photo sorter
DINOv3 + logistic regression
a small classifier on DINOv3 features keeps photos where a leaf is the main subject
→
3Level 1: leaf finder
YOLO26s detector, taught by Grounding DINO-base
YOLO is a fast object detector. A slow, large detector (the “teacher”) drew leaf boxes; the small YOLO (the “student”) was trained to draw the same boxes. It cuts out single leaves.
→
4Level 2: leaf-edge reader
YOLO26s-cls classifier on leaf crops
Looks at each cut-out leaf and gives a probability for smooth, toothed and lobed (e.g. toothed 0.9). Labels come from the field-guide table, so nobody labels photos by hand.
→
5Field-guide matching
Go Botany
An expert field guide: 546 woody species and their traits. For each trait, a species gets the log of the probability the reader gave to the value the guide lists for it; these are added over traits, and the species with the highest total is the answer.
→
6Answer
species + reasons
The name, plus ✓ or ✗ for each trait. If a trait conflicts with the guide, it says “please check”.

Training boxes: Grounding DINO-base (a detector you prompt with text, here “a leaf”). I browsed the boxes on all 716 test photos and saw no major problems; they have not yet been corrected one by one (see Next).

Why only 3 traits? Go Botany has 94 characters across all plant parts, about 10 of them leaf traits visible in photos. The first version read 3 core leaf traits (edge, simple/compound, leaves per node): most species have a single value for them and they are visible in a photo. The YOLO level-2 reader so far does leaf edge only.

Trait labels come from the field-guide table: if the guide says a species has a toothed edge, every photo of that species counts as toothed. We always test on species the models never saw in training.

How test species stay unseen. The 48 test species are fixed before any training: 24 like Quercus bicolor and Acer rubrum are in the field guide, but none of their photos is used in training; 24 like Morus rubra and Acer saccharum are fully held out, reserved for the future “learn a new species” loop. The code stops with an error if a test species appears in training (checked by name and iNaturalist taxon id). Test photos were uploaded in 2026.

Data: one expert table and three photo collections

Go Botanyfield-guide table, 546 woody species: source of trait labels and of the matching step
iNaturalist 20264,405 leaf photos: 368 training species (YOLO leaf-edge reader: a class-balanced subset of 262) and 48 unseen test species
BioImages1,641 hand-labelled photos: trains the leaf-photo sorter
Leafsnapsingle leaves on white, 185 northeastern US trees: next step for fine edges

Level 1: the small YOLO copies the teacher’s leaf boxes about 24× faster

The model is YOLO26s (Ultralytics YOLO26, small size). On photos of species it never saw, it reaches mAP50 = 0.875. mAP50 is, roughly, the share of the teacher’s boxes that the student also finds with a box overlapping it by at least half, averaged over confidence levels. The student needs 12 ms per photo; the teacher needs 287 ms.

Why train at all? Without training, the text-prompted YOLOE-26 finds 2.8 leaves per photo, against 12.0 for Grounding DINO-base (26 ms vs 287 ms).

Show untrained vs trained

Cost. One NVIDIA A10G GPU on Modal: about 15 min for 20 epochs, including image download; roughly US$0.3 at about $1.1 per GPU-hour (estimate). Level 2 trains in 1.1 min.

Caveats

  • The reference is the teacher’s boxes, so this measures imitation, not truth.
  • The best training round (epoch) was chosen on these same test photos, so the score is slightly optimistic.
  • Both teacher and student sometimes add one box covering almost the whole photo.

Level 2: YOLO reads the leaf edge at 0.83 on species it never saw

All rows are scored on the same 537 test photos of the 48 unseen species. Balanced accuracy: share read correctly, averaged over smooth, lobed and toothed (1.00 = perfect, 0.33 = guessing).

ModelLeaf edge (balanced accuracy)95% intervalNote
YOLO26s-cls, 1,024-px photos, 384-px input0.8250.72–0.90best; smooth 0.78 · lobed 0.94 · toothed 0.76
same, original photos, 640-px input0.8220.73–0.89smooth 0.81 vs 0.78, lobed 0.91 vs 0.94, toothed 0.74 vs 0.76: within one-run noise, no clear gain
Reference: BioCLIP features + small classifier, leaf crops0.860.76–0.93trained on 738 photos of 47 species

Intervals come from resampling the 37 test species that have a single leaf-edge value 2,000 times (photos of one species are not independent). They overlap: on this test set the three readers are not yet distinguishable. Three more training seeds: mean 0.811 (range 0.800–0.817).

Earlier attempt

The first full run did not learn (0.36, near chance even on its own training crops, 0.36). The likely cause is one of three setup differences (test crops stored in the training folder; minority classes balanced by copying crops; 5 instead of 3 crops per photo); it was fixed by changing all three.

Fairness. The YOLO run used 1,760 training photos (262 species); the BioCLIP reference used 738 photos (47 species), but BioCLIP may have seen these species during its pre-training. So the gap is not yet a fair comparison.

End to end: does the YOLO leaf-edge reason check the name?

The name is BioCLIP’s top guess. When the YOLO edge reason conflicts with the field guide for that name, the name is right only 77% of the time (vs 95% when it agrees), and the YOLO reason flags 14 of 49 wrong names vs 4 for the first-version reader. There are few wrong names, so treat this as a first sign.

Example: BioCLIP names a photo Fagus grandifolia; the guide says its leaf edge is toothed; if YOLO reads “toothed” the reason agrees, if it confidently reads “entire” the reason conflicts and the photo is flagged for checking.

BioCLIP + logistic regression57%6%37%94%90%4 / 49

Takeaway: better boxes (the planned hand-checked “pro” labels) and per-leaf labels address the sources behind 67% of the sampled errors.

What the first version already showed

1. A field-guide table is enough to teach traits, and more species help

Labels came only from species names plus the table, and the reader worked on unseen species. Training on more species (47 → 368) improved all three traits.

2. It explains its answers

For 95% of test photos the system can write a reason chain: all reasons fit (76%), or one does not and it asks you to check (19%).

Limitations

  • Only 48 test species (37 with a single leaf-edge value), so intervals are wide; finer comparisons need more test species.
  • Labels are per species from the field guide, so the test “truth” is itself noisy (see the error analysis). A hand-labelled, per-leaf test set would give the true accuracy.
  • The level-1 score uses the teacher’s boxes as reference, and the best epoch was picked on the test photos (a small optimistic bias).
  • Test photos are the ones the leaf-photo sorter kept (a leaf is the main subject); these may be easier than random field photos.
  • The YOLO and BioCLIP readers were trained on different photos (262 vs 47 species), so their comparison is indicative only.

Next: better boxes, more training, a fair comparison

  • Hand-checked “pro” boxes for level 1; retraining is cheap (about 25 GPU minutes).
  • Train level 2 on all photos and for more epochs, then compare YOLO and BioCLIP fairly on identical training data.
  • Leafsnap close-ups (single leaves on white) to teach fine leaf edges.
Appendix: method details
  • Scores. Trait scores are balanced accuracy: the share of photos read correctly, averaged over the trait’s values. Labels use only species with one recorded value. Models are logistic regressions on frozen image features (the big models are not changed). Test species are never in training (S4/S8). Leaf crops for the first version: Grounding DINO boxes on 1,024-px photos (S7). Two-level YOLO (S9/S10): Grounding DINO-base boxes on all photos (S9) train the YOLO26s detector; YOLO26s-cls is trained on the top-3 crops per photo with Go Botany leaf-edge labels; species in training and test never overlap. DINOv3 features were also tried for traits; BioCLIP was more stable, so it is shown. Leaf-photo sorter: DINOv3 classifier, threshold chosen on validation photos (S2).
  • How far can leaves alone go? (S0) Using the field guide only, with all traits read perfectly: with 4 core leaf traits, a median of 41 of the 546 species share the same traits, and the right species is in the top 5 for 35%; with all 10 leaf traits, 79%. So leaf reasons narrow the list a lot but rarely pin one species; that is why they are used as reasons next to a name.
  • Naming without reasons (S5). A general model already names these common species well: BioCLIP’s first guess is right for 93% of the 716 test photos. Our contribution is the reasons.
  • Evidence groups (S6). Supported 76%, conflict 19%, no evidence (the traits read do not separate the answer from other species) 5%.
